one_liner: Rust lock-free SPSC ring with built-in async push/pop; 1.29 vs 2.46 ns push+pop against rigtorp::SPSCQueue on Apple M4 Max.
what_it_does: Cynosure is a zero-dependency Rust crate of primitives for thread-per-core async executors (monoio, glommio); the catalogued part is site_d::ringbuf::RingBuf<T>, a bounded single-producer single-consumer queue. RingBuf::new(capacity) (power of two, non-zero-sized T) is split into a Producer and a Consumer that offer non-blocking try_push/try_pop, async push().await/pop().await, blocking variants, bulk slice copies, and std::io::Write/Read for u8. It is a Rust API with its own semantics, not a drop-in for rigtorp::SPSCQueue's emplace/front/pop interface.
how_it_is_fast: It is a Lamport ring with cached indices: each side keeps a private copy of the other side's index and reloads the shared atomic only when the ring looks full or empty, the two shared indices sit in separate 64-byte-aligned CachePadded cells, and power-of-two capacity turns wraparound into a mask (rigtorp::SPSCQueue wraps with a compare-and-reset over capacity+1 slots and splits a pop into front() plus pop()). Async support costs one SeqCst load of a waiter flag per operation (WaiterSlot::signal, inline(always), wake path cold-outlined), and the index publish is a SeqCst store; on AArch64 both compile to stlr/ldar with no dmb, per the source comments. Branch hints (likely/unlikely, taken from fereidani/branches) keep the full/empty checks off the hot path.
when_to_use: A fixed 1:1 stream between two tasks or cores on a thread-per-core executor (monoio, glommio), where the consumer should park with pop().await instead of spinning.
Small Copy payloads (u32-sized) at high rates on AArch64 (Apple silicon, Graviton-class servers), where the SeqCst publish costs the same as a release store.
Byte streams between threads through std::io::Write/Read on Producer<u8>/Consumer<u8>, or bulk slice transfers with try_push_slice/try_pop_slice.
Rust code that wants a single SPSC type with sync, blocking and async faces instead of combining a sync ring (rtrb, ringbuf-spsc) with a separate notification mechanism.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ code: the published lead over rigtorp::SPSCQueue (1.9x on one machine, single-thread push+pop) is not worth an FFI boundary, and the project's own hand-rolled C11 ring is 1.6x faster still.

x86-64 targets where the margin matters: every push and every pop ends with a SeqCst store, which the source notes 'carries the barrier' on x86, while rigtorp publishes with release stores; the file itself says x86 numbers are very different, and none are published.

Channels where either side may be dropped while the other waits: there is no closed flag or peer wake (open issue #2, 'close-on-drop semantics'), so pop().await or pop_blocking() on a ring whose producer is gone waits forever.
Multiple producers or consumers, or a shared work-stealing runtime with many senders: use mpsc_light or another channel; RingBuf is strictly SPSC.
Builds without LTO: the crate's Cargo.toml says its lean ops do not inline across the crate boundary without LTO and 'read artificially slow', so the published numbers assume release plus LTO.

integration.dependencies: none by default; optional monoio 0.2 (feature monoio-0_2)
integration.platforms: any std target; tuned and measured only on AArch64 (Apple M4 Max, macOS); no x86 numbers published
integration.thread_safety: Producer and Consumer are each Send (for T: Send) but not Sync: exactly one owner per side, usable from two different threads

gotchas: Harness flaw beyond the verifier's notes (C/C++ harness unpublished, flags unknown): the headline 1.29 ns and the repo's own criterion figure of 2.2 ns are the same u32 push+pop on the same M4 Max, so harness choice alone moves Cynosure by about 1.7x, close to the 1.9x margin claimed over rigtorp. That margin holds only if rigtorp ran in the identical unpublished loop, and rigtorp's pop() carries an assert that performs an extra acquire load of writeIdx_ unless NDEBUG is defined, which nobody can check here.

The C/C++ rows were added in the 0.6.0 commit 5f4601c (2026-07-27), after the 0.5.0 switch to SeqCst that fixed a cross-thread lost-wakeup deadlock; try_push and try_pop are unchanged between that commit and the 2026-09-21 hardening commit 2d44f34, so the numbers are not from stale or since-fixed hot-path code.

CachePadded is repr(align(64)), while crossbeam documents 128-byte lines on aarch64 big cores and pads to 128 there; on the benchmark's own M4 Max the read and write indices may share a 128-byte line in the two-thread rows. The single-thread latency row is unaffected.

Miri runs skip async tests (justfile: 'cargo +nightly miri test --lib -- --skip async'), so the async park and wake paths rely on loom and stress tests; push_slice/pop_slice futures are documented as not cancellation-safe (use the *_counted variants); capacity must be a power of two and zero-sized T panics.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Cynosure for in-process 1:1 handoff between cores on a thread-per-core Rust executor, where its async ring measured about 90 Melem/s cross-core against tokio mpsc's 15. Pick Myelon for cross-process shared-memory IPC, and Tokio's channels when you need multi-producer channels on a work-stealing runtime.
verified_claims_summary: On an Apple M4 Max under macOS, one u32 push plus one pop on a single thread took 1.29 ns for Cynosure's RingBuf, 2.46 ns for rigtorp::SPSCQueue (C++), 2.03 ns for ringbuffer-spsc and 0.79 ns for a hand-rolled C11 ring, in an unpublished tight-loop harness (LTO, DoNotOptimize) whose C/C++ compiler and flags are not stated. The repository's own criterion suite (Rust only, capacity 1024, bench profile with LTO) puts the same operation at 2.2 ns against rtrb's 2.5 ns.
status_note: Active single-author crate (0.7.0 published 2026-10-09, about 59.7k crates.io downloads, 3 stars, 42 commits) with a changelog that documents soundness fixes; MIT is declared in Cargo.toml and the README but the repo has no LICENSE file, and minor releases have broken APIs, so pin the version.
